title: Gaussian Flow Dynamics: Simulation-Free Neural SDE Learning Beyond One-Time Marginals

paper.title: Gaussian Flow Dynamics: Simulation-Free Neural SDE Learning Beyond One-Time Marginals
paper.abstract: Abstract Simulation-free training of latent Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) relies on a variational posterior process whose one-time marginals are tractable, typically Gaussian. Such marginals, however, do not determine the underlying dynamics: many processes share the same marginals while differing in their temporal structure, and existing parameterizations fix this structure implicitly, which restricts the posterior family and biases the learned model. We introduce Gaussian flow dynamics, which construct stochastic processes directly from smoothly evolving Gaussian marginals while making the marginal-preserving, or gauge, degrees of freedom explicit and parameterizable. The construction admits state-dependent diffusion coefficients and recovers every linear SDE with additive noise and a non-degenerate Gaussian initial distribution. Building on it, we propose Gauge Matching, a simulation-free method for latent SDE learning that combines Gaussian flow dynamics with the SDE Matching objective. Gauge Matching costs at most quadratically in the latent dimension per step, like SDE Matching, but learns the temporal structure of the posterior beyond its one-time marginals. It comes within a nat of Helmholtz- SDE , which computes the gauge from the prior Jacobian at cubic cost, on the linear benchmark where the exact posterior is known, matches it on nonlinear systems, and applies where Helmholtz- SDE does not, to state-dependent noise.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Neural or latent Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) model a time series as noisy observations of an unobserved state that evolves according to a learnable SDE ( Movellan et al., 2002 ; Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ; Hodgkinson et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , a natural choice for irregularly sampled, inherently stochastic dynamics, from neuroscience to fluid dynamics ( Course and Nair, 2023b ; Smith et al., 2026 ) . Training them requires the posterior over latent trajectories, which Variational Inference (VI) approximates with another SDE , the posterior process , whose drift depends on the data. Simulation-based methods integrate this process numerically at every gradient step ( Li et al., 2020 ) ; simulation-free methods ( Course and Nair, 2023a ; Bartosh et al., 2025 ) instead parameterize its one-time marginals, which can be sampled at any time, so that the objective becomes an expectation over a random time and state and a gradient step costs the same for any length of the series. The price of this efficiency is that the marginals underdetermine the process, and a method that parameterizes marginals still commits to one of the many processes that share them, implicitly. For Gaussian marginals, Course and Nair (2023a) ; Course and Nair (2023b) take the affine drift whose linear part is symmetric, and SDE Matching ( Bartosh et al., 2025 ) takes the drift induced by a particular square root of the covariance. Smith et al. (2026) recently showed that this choice, the gauge , is not benign: a fixed gauge restricts the variational family to a strict subset of the processes available to simulation-based methods, which degrades both inference and the learned dynamics when the posterior is uncertain. Their remedy, Helmholtz- SDE , keeps the marginals of SDE Matching and adds to its drift the marginal-preserving component of the difference between the prior and posterior drifts; the correction needs the Jacobian of the prior drift, costs at least cubically in the latent dimension, and requires state-independent noise. We make the gauge part of the parameterization. We introduce Gaussian flow dynamics , which build a stochastic process from a prescribed path of Gaussian marginals. Factorizing the square root of the covariance into a Cholesky factor and an orthogonal matrix separates the marginals from the gauge, which enters the dynamics only through a skew-symmetric generator that can be parameterized directly, at only quadratic cost and with state-dependent noise. We prove that the family is complete: it recovers every linear SDE with state-independent noise and a non-degenerate Gaussian initial distribution, and every marginal-preserving affine field is generated by such a skew-symmetric matrix. Building on this, we propose Gauge Matching , which combines Gaussian flow dynamics with the SDE Matching objective, so that the gauge is selected by the objective rather than by the parameterization. We characterize the selected gauge, in closed form for state-independent noise, and show that Helmholtz- SDE computes it for a linearized prior process with state-independent diffusion. Experimentally, the learned gauge removes most of the gap of the fixed gauges to the true posterior process in the linear-Gaussian (conjugate) setting, where that gap is available in closed form, matches Helmholtz- SDE on nonlinear systems at lower cost, improves on it when the prior drift is known and its linearization is poor, and extends to state-dependent noise, where Helmholtz- SDE does not apply. Section 6 discusses related work.

sections.heading: 3 Gaussian Flow Dynamics
sections.text: Gaussian flow dynamics are deterministic and stochastic dynamics constructed directly from a time-dependent affine transformation of a standard Gaussian, so that their marginals are the Gaussian laws it defines; the flow-map perspective exposes the degrees of freedom that are invisible from the marginals alone. sections.heading: 4 Gauge Matching
sections.text: Gauge Matching is SDE Matching with a Gaussian flow diffusion as posterior process, so that its marginals and its gauge are both learned, while the objective eq. 6 and its simulation-free estimator are unchanged. sections.heading: Relation to Helmholtz-SDE
sections.text: Helmholtz- SDE ( Smith et al., 2026 ) starts from a fixed-gauge posterior process with a state-independent diffusion coefficient and adds to its drift coefficient the q q -divergence-free component of the residual h − f h-f , which minimizes the path-space KL term over all marginal-preserving fields; to make it computable, the residual is replaced by its Taylor expansion about the mean m ⁡ ( t ) m(t) . At order ℓ = 1 \ell=1 , used in all their experiments, the correction is affine, hence a gauge field by Proposition 2 , and the corrected gauge is, irrespective of the fixed gauge it starts from, the solution of eq. 17 with the Jacobian at the mean, ∇ z h ​ ( t , m ) \nabla_{z}h(t,m) , in place of its expectation ( section C.2 ). The two gauges coincide whenever ∇ z h \nabla_{z}h is affine in z z , as for the quadratic Lorenz drift, and differ otherwise: Helmholtz- SDE finds the optimal gauge of the linearized prior process, whereas Gauge Matching minimizes the exact objective over the same family; only corrections of order ℓ ≥ 2 \ell\geq 2 leave it, and a state-dependent gauge generator recovers those as well, still simulation-free ( section B.1 ). The larger difference is computational. Solving eq. 17 at every evaluation requires the Jacobian of the prior drift network and 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(d^{3}) linear algebra, and for a state-dependent diffusion coefficient it becomes a linear system whose coefficients must be estimated numerically ( section C.2 ). Gauge Matching learns Ω ϕ \Omega_{\phi} by stochastic gradient descent, at 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 2 ) \mathcal{O}(d^{2}) , without derivatives of the prior drift coefficient and for state-dependent diffusion coefficients ( table 1 ). Since 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is strictly convex in Ω \Omega , the optimal gauge is a unique target at every ( t , X ) (t,X) ; Ω ϕ \Omega_{\phi} may still have local optima in ϕ \phi , as any network does, but in section 5 gradient descent reaches the optimal gauge. The family with a learned gauge can. Corollary 4 (Conjugate Setting) . Let the prior process be the linear SDE eq. 12 with S 0 ∈ GL ⁡ ( d ) S_{0}\in\operatorname{GL}(d) and Σ ⁡ ( t ) \Sigma(t) positive definite, and let p θ ​ ( x ∣ z ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( x ∣ C ​ z , R ) p_{\theta}(x\mid z)=\mathcal{N}(x\mid Cz,R) with R R positive definite. Then (i) between consecutive observation times, the true posterior process is a Gaussian flow diffusion with diffusion coefficient g g , continuously differentiable m m , L L and continuous Ω \Omega ; and (ii) the infimum of the KL divergence from Gauge Matching posterior processes to the true one is zero (proof in section C.3 ). sections.heading: Noisy Lorenz Attractor
sections.text: We follow Smith et al. (2026) : the stochastic Lorenz system on [ 0 , 5 ] [0,5] , with process noise large enough that the posterior does not collapse onto the true trajectory, is observed every Δ ​ t = 0.25 \Delta t=0.25 through a noisy linear map, for 1024 training trials; the latent SDE has d = 4 d=4 , a neural prior drift and a fixed diffusion coefficient, and the prior and observation model are learned jointly with the posterior process. In table 2 , the fixed gauges reach a negative ELBO of 75 75 – 78 78 nats per trial, whether with diagonal or with full covariance. Gauge Matching and Helmholtz- SDE reach 53 53 nats; the difference lies in the path-space KL term, and their marginals assign a higher likelihood to the true latent state. The learned dynamics improve too: the autocorrelation error of the prior process drops from 0.11 0.11 – 0.13 0.13 to 0.05 0.05 – 0.06 0.06 , and only these two models reproduce the outward spiral within each lobe of the attractor ( fig. 8 ). The gauge excess confirms that gradient descent finds the optimal gauge, to within 0.05 0.05 nats per unit time against 2.5 2.5 – 2.8 2.8 for the fixed gauges, and the last row shows that the gain is the gauge, not the covariance: a diagonal L ϕ L_{\phi} with a learned gauge reaches 55.3 55.3 nats, a full L ϕ L_{\phi} without one stays at 75.5 75.5 . The picture holds across observation spacings and noise levels ( appendix D ), and the agreement of Gauge Matching and Helmholtz- SDE is what section 4 predicts: the fitted drift networks are nearly affine over the posterior support.

sections.heading: Known Nonlinear Drift
sections.text: Gauge Matching and Helmholtz- SDE differ when the prior drift is known and strongly nonlinear: on a Stuart–Landau oscillator with shear and the generative model fixed at the truth ( table 4 in appendix D ), the gauge excess of the learned gauge is 10 10 times smaller than that of the order-one correction, and its negative ELBO is lower by 1.6 ± 0.3 1.6\pm 0.3 nats, on every seed.

sections.heading: State-Dependent Noise
sections.text: The stochastic Lotka–Volterra system ( Vadillo, 2019 ; Bartosh et al., 2025 ) has multiplicative noise, g ⁡ ( z ) = σ ​ diag ⁡ ( z ) g(z)=\sigma\operatorname{diag}(z) , which Helmholtz- SDE does not support; in log coordinates the noise becomes additive and the drift acquires exponentials. We learn a latent SDE from sparse, noisy observations in each coordinate system, with the true diffusion coefficient in log coordinates and a learned state-dependent one in the original ones, and evaluate the learned prior process by the period of its cycle, the predator’s lag behind the prey and the autocorrelation error ( table 5 in appendix D ). In log coordinates the posterior is narrow relative to the curvature of the drift, so the order-one correction is already optimal: Helmholtz- SDE and Gauge Matching agree, as section 4 predicts, with gauge excess 0.000 0.000 and 0.004 0.004 against 0.215 0.215 for the fixed gauge. In the original coordinates, where Helmholtz- SDE does not apply, Gauge Matching reduces the period error from 22 % 22\% to 13 % 13\% and improves all three metrics on every seed ( fig. 10 ). The same holds in d = 8 d=8 : on a rotating Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with multiplicative noise g ⁡ ( z ) = σ ​ diag ⁡ ( 1 + z i 2 ) g(z)=\sigma\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{1+z_{i}^{2}}) , Gauge Matching lowers the negative ELBO of the fixed gauges by 6.6 ± 0.8 6.6\pm 0.8 nats with the generative model known and 4.8 ± 0.3 4.8\pm 0.3 with a learned prior, at an 18 18 – 29 29 times smaller gauge excess ( table 6 ).

sections.heading: Variational Inference for Latent SDEs
sections.text: Simulation-based VI parameterizes the posterior process by its drift coefficient and optimizes the gauge implicitly, at the cost of one numerical integration per gradient step: with an affine drift the marginals follow from moment ODEs ( Archambeau et al., 2007a ; Archambeau et al., 2007b ; Duncker et al., 2019 ; Wildner and Koeppl, 2021 ; Köhs et al., 2021 ; Verma et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025 ) ; with a neural drift the process is simulated and differentiated through ( Movellan et al., 2002 ; Ryder et al., 2018 ; Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ; Hodgkinson et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2020 ; Kidger et al., 2021 ) , as in latent ODEs ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Rubanova et al., 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Simulation-Free Methods and the Gauge
sections.text: Diffusions with prescribed marginals go back to Brigo (2000) ; Brigo (2002) and were used for variational path estimation by Sutter et al. (2016) . Simulation-free VI with Gaussian marginals ( Course and Nair, 2023a ; Course and Nair, 2023b ; Bartosh et al., 2025 ) fixes the gauge ( appendix B ); Kiyohara et al. (2025) use a mean-field family, and Neklyudov et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2024) learn simulation-free dynamics in observation space. Smith et al. (2026) identified a post-hoc gauge correction ( section 4 ) and briefly mention learning Ω \Omega in their Appendix A.5 without developing or evaluating it; they suggest this sacrifices SDE Matching’s closed-form structure, whereas our O ⁡ ( t ) O(t) construction retains its explicit closed-form flow map.

sections.heading: Marginal-Preserving Fields
sections.text: The same freedom appears in generative modeling, where the probability-flow ODE ( Song et al., 2021 ) is one of many transports between the marginals of a diffusion model: Horvat and Pfister (2024) analyze this freedom, Petrović et al. (2025) exploit it in flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) to learn non-gradient dynamics, and Hua et al. (2025) parameterize a density and a dynamics jointly so that the continuity equation holds by construction. Helmholtz–Hodge decompositions also structure Gaussian-process models of vector fields ( Berlinghieri et al., 2023 ; Xu and Pan, 2024 ) . There the divergence-free component is a modeling choice; here it is a coordinate of the variational family that the marginals leave free. Diffusion models with learned noising processes ( Singhal et al., 2023 ; Bartosh et al., 2024a ; Nielsen et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Bartosh et al., 2024b ; Du et al., 2024 ) are latent SDEs with one observation and a learned posterior.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Gaussian flow dynamics, which turn the marginal-preserving freedom of a process with Gaussian marginals into an explicit skew-symmetric generator, at quadratic cost and for state-dependent diffusion coefficients, and Gauge Matching, which lets the SDE Matching objective select this generator. The learned gauge removes most of the gap of the fixed gauges in the conjugate setting, matches Helmholtz- SDE on nonlinear systems at lower cost and up to d = 64 d=64 , improves on it when the prior drift is known and strongly nonlinear, and extends to state-dependent noise, where Helmholtz- SDE does not apply. A state-dependent gauge generator extends the construction to general nonlinear marginal-preserving fields, beyond the polynomial gauges and state-independent diffusion of Helmholtz- SDE ( section B.1 ); its evaluation and non-Gaussian marginals are left for future work.

sections.text: For all three fixed gauges, Cholesky, square root and symmetric, the gauge is a deterministic function of the marginals and Σ \Sigma , chosen independently of the objective. In Gauge Matching, Ω ⁡ ( t ) \Omega(t) is instead a free function, and Proposition 2 shows that no other affine choice exists: every fixed gauge is a point in the family we optimize over. One special case matters for section 5.1 . When the marginals are stationary, P ˙ = 0 \dot{P}=0 , the Cholesky and square root gauges give K = 0 K=0 , and the symmetric gauge gives K = 0 K=0 as well whenever Σ \Sigma and P P commute, as in the isotropic setting there. This appendix lists the choices shared by all experiments and then, for each experiment, the data, the model, deviations of the posterior process from the shared architecture, the training schedule, and the definition of every reported metric. Posterior architecture. All posterior processes share the amortized architecture of Bartosh et al. (2025) : a GRU processes the observations of a trial into per-observation embeddings (when the observation times are irregular, it also receives the times and their spacings); the embedding at a query time t t is a softmax-weighted average of these, with weights centered at t t over the observation times; and an MLP with two hidden layers of width 100 and SiLU activations maps the embedding and t t to the posterior parameters. sections.heading: Gap and Gauge Excess
sections.text: Two quantities recur in the experiments. The gap of a fitted posterior process is its KL divergence to the true posterior process ( section 5.1 ). For two processes with a common diffusion coefficient this divergence is, by Girsanov’s theorem, an initial KL term plus a path-space term (the display in Step 3 of section C.3 ). When both drift coefficients are affine, as for a linear prior process and every posterior process considered here, the integrand of the path-space term is a Gaussian expectation of a quadratic form, and we evaluate the gap in closed form on a time grid of step 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} . The gauge excess of table 2 is 𝒥 ⁡ ( Ω ) − 𝒥 ⁡ ( Ω ⋆ ) \mathcal{J}(\Omega)-\mathcal{J}(\Omega^{\star}) in nats per unit time, where 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is the integrand of Proposition 3 at the marginals of the trained model, Ω \Omega is the gauge the method uses at each time t t , and Ω ⋆ \Omega^{\star} is the solution of eq. 17 with the expected Jacobian estimated from 10 3 10^{3} Monte Carlo samples; 𝒥 \mathcal{J} itself is estimated from the same samples. The result is averaged over t t on a grid of 100 100 points and over 64 64 held-out trials; every gauge excess reported below uses this estimator. Since 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is a strictly convex quadratic function of Ω \Omega , the excess is nonnegative, and it is zero exactly when the method’s gauge is the optimal one for its own marginals.

sections.text: Data. Training. 3 ⋅ 10 4 3\cdot 10^{4} iterations, batches of 256 trials, learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , for all methods. Metrics. The negative ELBO is eq. 6 per test trial. For lags τ \tau on a grid of step 0.05 0.05 in [ 0 , 2 ] [0,2] , we form the 3 × 3 3\times 3 correlation matrix of the observed coordinates between times t t and t + τ t+\tau , average the squared Frobenius distance to the corresponding matrix of the true prior process over t t and τ \tau , and report the root mean square over entries. The Monte Carlo floor of this estimator at this sample size is 0.024 0.024 , and the true dynamics started from the fitted posterior at t = 0 t=0 score 0.030 0.030 ; the gauge-corrected models, at 0.052 0.052 – 0.056 0.056 , are therefore within 0.03 0.03 of what the estimator can resolve. Figure 8 shows sample paths of each learned prior process against the true one. The gauge excess is defined above. The training time quoted in section 5.2 is the wall-clock time to 3 ⋅ 10 4 3\cdot 10^{4} iterations, averaged over seeds; the five methods shared one GPU, so only ratios are meaningful: relative to SDE Matching, the Cholesky gauge, the symmetric gauge, Helmholtz- SDE and Gauge Matching took 1.06 1.06 , 1.27 1.27 , 1.43 1.43 and 1.17 1.17 times as long. Comparison with published numbers. Our negative ELBO values are 6 6 – 10 10 nats above those reported by Smith et al. (2026) for the same methods, uniformly across methods, so the differences between SDE Matching and Helmholtz- SDE agree with theirs. The offset is not overfitting, since training and test values agree to within 1 1 nat; it is consistent with a difference in batch size or data draw and, for SDE Matching, with our use of the fixed diffusion coefficient. Robustness to observation spacing and noise. We repeat the experiment for the observation spacings Δ ​ t ∈ { 0.125 , 0.25 , 0.5 } \Delta t\in\{0.125,0.25,0.5\} , that is N = 41 N=41 , 21 21 or 11 11 observations per trial on [ 0 , 5 ] [0,5] , and the observation noise levels σ ∈ { 0.15 , 0.3 , 0.6 } \sigma\in\{0.15,0.3,0.6\} ; ( 0.25 , 0.3 ) (0.25,0.3) is the protocol of table 2 . Why the drift must be known. With a learned prior drift, Gauge Matching and Helmholtz- SDE coincide on every system we tried, including van der Pol and Stuart–Landau oscillators: a drift network fitted through posteriors as wide as those encountered here is close to affine over the posterior support, its expected Jacobian equals its Jacobian at the mean to 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and the order-one correction is exact for it. This, and not the degree of the true drift, is why the Lorenz and Lotka–Volterra systems do not separate the two methods. Which oscillator. Naesseth Affiliation: Informatics Institute Affiliation: University of Amsterdam Email: christian.a.naesseth@uva.nl Abstract Simulation-free training of latent Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) relies on a variational posterior process whose one-time marginals are tractable, typically Gaussian. Such marginals, however, do not determine the underlying dynamics: many processes share the same marginals while differing in their temporal structure, and existing parameterizations fix this structure implicitly, which restricts the posterior family and biases the learned model. We introduce Gaussian flow dynamics, which construct stochastic processes directly from smoothly evolving Gaussian marginals while making the marginal-preserving, or gauge, degrees of freedom explicit and parameterizable. The construction admits state-dependent diffusion coefficients and recovers every linear SDE with additive noise and a non-degenerate Gaussian initial distribution. Building on it, we propose Gauge Matching, a simulation-free method for latent SDE learning that combines Gaussian flow dynamics with the SDE Matching objective. Gauge Matching costs at most quadratically in the latent dimension per step, like SDE Matching, but learns the temporal structure of the posterior beyond its one-time marginals. It comes within a nat of Helmholtz- SDE , which computes the gauge from the prior Jacobian at cubic cost, on the linear benchmark where the exact posterior is known, matches it on nonlinear systems, and applies where Helmholtz- SDE does not, to state-dependent noise. 1 Introduction Neural or latent Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) model a time series as noisy observations of an unobserved state that evolves according to a learnable SDE ( Movellan et al., 2002 ; Tzen and Raginsky, 2019 ; Hodgkinson et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , a natural choice for irregularly sampled, inherently stochastic dynamics, from neuroscience to fluid dynamics ( Course and Nair, 2023b ; Smith et al., 2026 ) . Training them requires the posterior over latent trajectories, which Variational Inference (VI) approximates with another SDE , the posterior process , whose drift depends on the data. Simulation-based methods integrate this process numerically at every gradient step ( Li et al., 2020 ) ; simulation-free methods ( Course and Nair, 2023a ; Bartosh et al., 2025 ) instead parameterize its one-time marginals, which can be sampled at any time, so that the objective becomes an expectation over a random time and state and a gradient step costs the same for any length of the series. The price of this efficiency is that the marginals underdetermine the process, and a method that parameterizes marginals still commits to one of the many processes that share them, implicitly. For Gaussian marginals, Course and Nair (2023a) ; Course and Nair (2023b) take the affine drift whose linear part is symmetric, and SDE Matching ( Bartosh et al., 2025 ) takes the drift induced by a particular square root of the covariance. Smith et al. (2026) recently showed that this choice, the gauge , is not benign: a fixed gauge restricts the variational family to a strict subset of the processes available to simulation-based methods, which degrades both inference and the learned dynamics when the posterior is uncertain. Their remedy, Helmholtz- SDE , keeps the marginals of SDE Matching and adds to its drift the marginal-preserving component of the difference between the prior and posterior drifts; the correction needs the Jacobian of the prior drift, costs at least cubically in the latent dimension, and requires state-independent noise. We make the gauge part of the parameterization. We introduce Gaussian flow dynamics , which build a stochastic process from a prescribed path of Gaussian marginals. Factorizing the square root of the covariance into a Cholesky factor and an orthogonal matrix separates the marginals from the gauge, which enters the dynamics only through a skew-symmetric generator that can be parameterized directly, at only quadratic cost and with state-dependent noise. We prove that the family is complete: it recovers every linear SDE with state-independent noise and a non-degenerate Gaussian initial distribution, and every marginal-preserving affine field is generated by such a skew-symmetric matrix. Building on this, we propose Gauge Matching , which combines Gaussian flow dynamics with the SDE Matching objective, so that the gauge is selected by the objective rather than by the parameterization. We characterize the selected gauge, in closed form for state-independent noise, and show that Helmholtz- SDE computes it for a linearized prior process with state-independent diffusion. Experimentally, the learned gauge removes most of the gap of the fixed gauges to the true posterior process in the linear-Gaussian (conjugate) setting, where that gap is available in closed form, matches Helmholtz- SDE on nonlinear systems at lower cost, improves on it when the prior drift is known and its linearization is poor, and extends to state-dependent noise, where Helmholtz- SDE does not apply.
